To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) P450 and other oxygenases have chains of tryptophan and tyrosine that extend to protein surfaces and (2) hole tunneling (hole hopping) through these chains is the primary mechanism of survival for high-valent iron oxo and other reactive oxygen species.

(i) the oxygenation of inert organic compounds by P450 enzymes involves high-valent iron-oxos; (ii) the iron–oxos in P450s are strong oxidants; and (iii) P450 enzymes have chains of tyrosl and tryptophanyl residues that are designed to guide the oxidizing hole to protein surfaces where it is quenched

(a) high-valent iron-oxo survival times are a function of the distance of the nearest Tyr/Trp residue to the hemo, (b) Tyr/Trp hole hopping maps can be calculated, (c) the Tyr/Trp chain distances are a function of evolutionary history, and (d) this evolutionary history is a function of O2 concentration.
